questions.stem: A 73-year-old woman who resides in a skilled nursing care facility is brought to the emergency department after she was found lethargic and minimally responsive 30 minutes ago. She has had a 3-day history of vomiting and has not produced urine during the past 24 hours. She was hospitalized for pneumonia 3 weeks ago. She has renal insufficiency, type 2 diabetes mellitus, congestive heart failure, and dementia. Her medications are furosemide, metformin, and memantine. She has no known allergies. On arrival, the patient moans incoherently to questions or stimulation. Her temperature is 35.4°C (95.7°F), pulse is 82/min and regular, respirations are 25/min, and blood pressure is 90/43 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 93%. The skin is cool and clammy to touch. Crackles are heard at the lung bases. The abdomen is soft; there is mild, diffuse tenderness to palpation. There is moderate pitting edema of the lower extremities. She is able to move all four extremities, but she does not cooperate with a neurologic examination. Fingerstick blood glucose concentration is 78 mg/dL (4.33 mmol/L). An ECG is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
The ECG has findings consistent with hyperkalemia, and this patient requires immediate intervention to decrease the risk for a fatal arrhythmia. ECG evidence of hyperkalemia includes flattening of the P-waves, lengthening of the PR interval, widening of the QRS complex, and the presence of tall, peaked T-waves. Acute management in order of priority involves stabilization of the myocardium with calcium gluconate or calcium chloride, shifting serum potassium into the intracellular compartment (using insulin and

dextrose, sodium bicarbonate, or β-adrenergic agonists), and removal of potassium from the body (using diuretics, oral potassium binders, or hemodialysis). After the patient is stabilized, evaluation should be directed toward identifying the cause of the hyperkalemia. In this patient with a recent hospitalization for pneumonia, dementia, underlying chronic kidney injury, loop diuretic use, and recent history of emesis, the most likely explanation is acute on chronic renal failure caused by hypovolemia exacerbated by diuretic use. Next steps include laboratory studies, urinalysis, imaging, and admission for further management.

wrongAnswers.A: Aspirin (Choice A) is not indicated in the acute management of hyperkalemia. The ECG does not show ST-segment elevations or evidence of ischemic injury that would warrant antiplatelet therapy at this time.
wrongAnswers.C: Dextrose (Choice C), combined with insulin, is indicated for management of hyperkalemia but does not take precedence over calcium gluconate. The role of dextrose is to prevent hypoglycemia when insulin is administered. Insulin promotes the shift of potassium from the extracellular space to the intracellular compartment, decreasing the serum potassium concentration.
wrongAnswers.D: Dopamine (Choice D), or another vasopressor with β-adrenergic activity, may be required if the patient has persistent shock after correction of hyperkalemia and resolution of ECG changes. β-Adrenergic vasopressors also carry a risk for inducing further tachyarrhythmias that may worsen the patient’s condition. Calcium gluconate is the priority.
wrongAnswers.E: Furosemide (Choice E) may be trialed in this patient in combination with intravenous fluids to decrease the total body potassium concentration by blocking absorption of potassium in the loop of Henle. Calcium gluconate and attempts to shift potassium into the intracellular department should be initiated first. The presence of anuria for 24 hours may also prevent furosemide from being effective, and acute hemodialysis should be considered if the hyperkalemia persists and she remains anuric.
wrongAnswers.F: Naloxone (Choice F) generally provides potential benefit with low risk for harm when treating encephalopathy, respiratory depression, or hypotension caused by suspected opioid overdose. This patient does not have opioid toxicity findings such as bradypnea or miosis, and the ECG is concerning for hyperkalemia requiring immediate calcium.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by paramedics 15 minutes after he was involved in a motor vehicle collision in which he was the restrained driver. The patient was traveling at about 5 miles per hour (8 km/hr) in a parking lot when his car struck a parked vehicle. Paramedics say that the damage to both vehicles was minimal. The patient says he consumed two beers earlier in the evening. On arrival, he is awake, alert, and fully oriented. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Examination shows tenderness and swelling of the right elbow but no other abnormalities. The physician recommends that an x-ray of the elbow be performed. The patient says that he would prefer to leave; he is able to verbalize the risks of leaving using his own words. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences

explanationPanel.correct: A. Allow the patient to leave against medical advice
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Patient autonomy is one of four common medical ethical principles, along with beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice. Autonomy posits that patients have the right to make their decisions provided that they have the capacity to do so and that they have been provided with appropriate information for use in making such a decision. A consenting adult with decision-making capacity has the right to refuse some or all aspects of medical care even if such a decision may result in short- or long-term morbidity or mortality. In this case, the patient is declining further work-up and treatment of a musculoskeletal injury induced by a motor vehicle collision. Provided that this patient has capacity and that the caring physician has explained the benefits, risks, and alternatives of not performing the x-ray of the elbow, the patient may elect to refuse and then be allowed to leave against medical advice.

wrongAnswers.B: It is not necessary to call the police (Choice B) in this case because the patient has decision-making capacity, there is no evidence that he poses an imminent danger to himself or others, and the recommended elbow x-ray is not legally mandatory.
wrongAnswers.C: Detaining the patient until his blood alcohol concentration is measured (Choice C) or obtaining x-rays despite the patient’s wishes (Choice E) violates the ethical principle of patient autonomy. Because this patient demonstrates decision-making capacity by being able to verbalize the risks of leaving in his own words (and is not suspected to be impaired), there is no justification to detain the patient or perform tests against his will.
wrongAnswers.D: It is not appropriate for the physician to make a diagnosis without adequate information to support that diagnosis in order to appease a patient. Thus, discharging the patient with a diagnosis of elbow contusion (Choice D) is not the correct course of action. If the physician is recommending further work-up and the patient chooses to leave the emergency department instead, he will do so against medical advice, and a mutually agreed upon discharge should not occur even if the diagnosis is correct.
wrongAnswers.E: Detaining the patient until his blood alcohol concentration is measured (Choice C) or obtaining x-rays despite the patient’s wishes (Choice E) violates the ethical principle of patient autonomy. questions.stem: A previously healthy 60-year-old Hispanic woman is brought to the emergency department by her son because of a 1-week history of cough and low-grade fever. She understands some English but does not speak it fluently. Her son speaks fluent English and Spanish. The physician is not fluent in Spanish but can communicate limitedly with the patient. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 140/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. Breath sounds are decreased at the lung bases with occasional rhonchi that clear with cough. An x-ray of the chest shows no evidence of pneumonia; however, a 1-cm mass that requires follow-up is noted in the left lower lobe. An ECG shows normal sinus rhythm and no evidence of ischemic changes. The patient is anxious to leave, and the hospital interpreter is with another patient. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to communicate the need for further evaluation of a potential malignancy?

explanationPanel.correct: D. Wait for the interpreter before issuing the discharge instructions
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Waiting for the interpreter before issuing the discharge instructions is the appropriate action in this scenario. Professional interpreters can provide high-quality translations that maintain patient safety. Credentialed interpreters are trained in medical knowledge and vocabulary, ethics, and cultural sensitivity. Relying on a family member for interpreting increases the risk for miscommunication about medical or culturally relevant details and can jeopardize informed consent for treatment and patient safety. This is important for all care, but particularly so in this case because a miscommunication could jeopardize a timely diagnosis of malignancy in this patient.

wrongAnswers.A: Asking the son to translate the discharge instructions to the patient (Choice A) or giving the discharge instructions directly to the son (Choice C) is not appropriate. Family members should not be used as interpreters for important medical information because this increases the risk for miscommunication and can jeopardize informed consent and patient safety.
wrongAnswers.B: Calling the patient's primary care physician to communicate the information (Choice B) or writing down the discharge instructions in English and asking the patient to give them to her primary care physician (Choice E) are both inappropriate because they displace the responsibility of the patient’s care onto someone else. While the patient’s primary care provider should be notified of the patient’s visit and the need for malignancy work-up, the burden of sharing this with the patient is the responsibility of the emergency department physician via a professional interpreter.

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Anaphylactic shock, a severe type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reaction, presents following exposure to an allergen. It is caused by widespread IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation and is characterized by histaminergic responses within multiple organ systems leading to flushing, angioedema, bronchospasm, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, and vasodilation, which can lead to airway obstruction and circulatory collapse. It is generally acute in onset following a specific exposure and generally does not self-resolve. If not managed promptly, death can occur from hypoxia and/or distributive shock. Anaphylaxis is a form of distributive shock, which is characterized by a primary reduction in systemic vascular resistance (SVR). This reduction in SVR is secondary to IgE-mediated histamine and cytokine release. Cardiac output increases to compensate for low SVR in the early stages of distributive shock. If the inciting state is not appropriately treated, further decompensation can occur, resulting in progressive hypotension and insufficient perfusion with associated end-organ damage. After the administration of epinephrine, fluid resuscitation should be initiated to increase intravascular volume to support adequate organ perfusion.

wrongAnswers.A: Acute serum sickness (Choice A) is a type III (immune complex-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction in which antibodies to foreign proteins are produced and immune complexes deposit in membranes, leading to tissue damage. It typically presents with fever, urticaria, arthralgias, proteinuria, and lymphadenopathy 5 to 10 days after exposure. Anaphylaxis is typically an immediate and acute reaction.
wrongAnswers.C: Cardiogenic shock (Choice C) can occur in diseases such as myocarditis, acute myocardial infarction, and congestive heart failure. In cardiogenic shock, there is severe dysfunction of the cardiac myocytes resulting in markedly decreased contractility, tachycardia, hypotension, and impaired end-organ perfusion (cool extremities and low urine output).
wrongAnswers.D: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (Choice D) presents with bleeding, thrombocytopenia, increased prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times, decreased plasma fibrinogen concentration, and increased d-dimer and fibrin split product concentration. It can be caused by trauma, severe sepsis, and occasionally malignancy. It is unlikely to cause hypotension unless the patient is experiencing severe bleeding resulting in hemorrhagic shock or refractory sepsis.
wrongAnswers.E: Septic shock (Choice E) is characterized by vasoplegia (impaired response of the vasculature to vasoconstricting stimuli) with markedly decreased systemic vascular resistance, which can cause hypotension and tachycardia. However, sepsis typically occurs because of an overwhelming bacterial infection, and this patient’s immediate and acute symptoms are more likely caused by antigen exposure and anaphylaxis.

explanationPanel.rule: Immediate hypotension, hypoxemia, flushing, and obtundation after antivenom = anaphylaxis/distributive shock.
explanationPanel.trap: Serum sickness occurs days later with fever, rash/urticaria, arthralgias, and immune-complex findings, not minutes later with shock.

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
The patient’s presentation is most consistent with sepsis complicated by distributive shock. Sepsis is a systemic inflammatory syndrome that results from a dysregulated and exaggerated immune response to an infection. Sepsis can be complicated by shock and multiorgan failure with a high mortality rate. Septic shock is characterized by vasoplegia

(impaired response of the vasculature to vasoconstricting stimuli) with markedly decreased systemic vascular resistance, increased cardiac output (tachycardia, hyperdynamic ventricular function), oliguria, and lactic acidosis. Fever, tachypnea, and leukocytosis also support a diagnosis of sepsis. Hypotension, cool mottled extremities, and end-organ dysfunction indicate the presence of shock. The patient’s risk for developing a severe infection is increased by use of daily corticosteroids and a tumor necrosis factor α blocker for her rheumatoid arthritis.

wrongAnswers.A: Cardiac tamponade (Choice A) can result in obstructive shock caused by compression of the cardiac chambers. Findings suggestive of cardiac tamponade include hypotension, jugular venous distention, distant heart sounds, pulsus paradoxus, and a low-voltage ECG.
wrongAnswers.B: Gastrointestinal bleeding (Choice B) may result in hemorrhagic/hypovolemic shock, and the use of ibuprofen and corticosteroids are risk factors for gastrointestinal bleeding. The presence of fever and leukocytosis and the absence of any reported history of bleeding make sepsis a more likely diagnosis. The initial management for both septic and hemorrhagic shock is fluid resuscitation.
wrongAnswers.C: Non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction (Choice C) may lead to cardiogenic shock because of impaired ventricular contraction and inadequate cardiac output. Typical findings include jugular venous distention, pulmonary crackles, and a weak pulse. Measuring troponin concentration and performing echocardiography can support or refute the diagnosis.
wrongAnswers.D: Pulmonary embolism (Choice D) can cause an obstructive form of shock in which the right ventricle fails as it contracts against greater resistance in the pulmonary vasculature. This results in diminished left heart return and cardiac output, with the consequence of decreased perfusion to the right ventricle and further loss of function.

explanationPanel.educationalObjective: Septic shock refers to the presence of persistent hypoperfusion despite adequate fluid resuscitation in the setting of infection. It is characterized by vasoplegia and increased cardiac stroke volume and pulse, and it may progress to multi-organ dysfunction.
explanationPanel.rule: Fever, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, hypotension, hyperdynamic precordium, and infection risk = sepsis with distributive shock.
explanationPanel.trap: Tamponade/PE/cardiogenic shock cause obstructive or pump failure patterns, not infectious SIRS with vasoplegia and high-output physiology.

If this patient is discharged, which of the following historical factors most increases her risk of attempting suicide?

questions.subject: Psychiatry

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Suicide is the most serious and acute risk for patients with depression, so physicians should ask detailed questions about patients’ suicidal ideation and recent or remote suicide attempts when there is any suggestion of suicidality. Suicidality differs by gender: women are more likely to attempt suicide while men are less likely to attempt suicide but more likely to be successful when they do so. Other risk factors for suicide attempts include age over 45 years, previous attempts, alcohol or other substance abuse, chronic illness, an organized plan or access to weapons, being unmarried, and a lack of social support. In this case, the patient’s excessive alcohol use is the factor that most increases her risk for attempting suicide, which is a modifiable risk factor. When evaluating a patient with suicidal ideation, the physician should conduct a full psychiatric assessment and ask the patient directly about their intent and plan to commit suicide while also assessing overall risk using a validated suicide risk assessment scale. Any patient at moderate to high risk warrants further assessment by a trained psychiatrist, psychologist, or mental health worker and consideration for admission. If a patient in such a case is discharged, a contract for safety and safe discharge plan should be established with the patient.

wrongAnswers.A: While age over 45 years is associated with suicide attempts, this patient’s age of 29 years is not (Choice A).
wrongAnswers.C: Family and spousal support, which this patient has, is a strongly protective factor for suicide. Thus, family support (Choice C) is not a risk factor for this patient attempting suicide.
wrongAnswers.D: This patient’s female gender (Choice D) is slightly associated with an increased risk for attempting suicide, but her alcohol abuse is a stronger risk factor in this case.
wrongAnswers.E: Occupation (Choice E) does impact suicide risk, but this patient’s occupation of insurance agent is not among the occupations at higher risk for suicide. Suicide risk increases among unskilled workers compared with skilled workers. However, among highly skilled workers, physicians may be at increased risk for suicide.

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Alcohol increases the central nervous system activity of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), the main inhibitory neurotransmitter. Abrupt discontinuation of alcohol therefore leads to sympathetic (excitatory) excess. Uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal typically presents with tremors, anxiety, restlessness, headache, nausea, and diaphoresis, which can occur hours after the cessation of alcohol use. If left untreated, alcohol withdrawal can also be complicated by seizures and alcoholic hallucinosis (auditory or visual hallucinations). Delirium tremens, the most concerning and life-threatening complication of alcohol withdrawal, involves severe confusion and disorientation, fluctuations in consciousness, agitation, visual hallucinations, and autonomic instability (fluctuations in pulse and blood pressure with hyperthermia). Alcohol withdrawal is managed supportively with benzodiazepines (eg, lorazepam) to address agitation and prevent the symptoms of withdrawal, along with fluids, nutritional supplementation, and frequent assessment including vital sign checks.

wrongAnswers.A: Administration of dextrose and vitamin B (thiamine) (Choice A) may be helpful in this patient with chronic alcohol use disorder because of malnutrition, but it is more useful for treatment of Wernicke encephalopathy. This patient is presenting with alcohol withdrawal, making treatment with benzodiazepines more appropriate.
wrongAnswers.C: Administration of phenytoin (Choice C) would be appropriate in cases of epilepsy, but this patient’s seizure is likely provoked by alcohol withdrawal and should be treated with benzodiazepines.
wrongAnswers.D: CT scan of the head (Choice D) would be appropriate in the evaluation of first-time unprovoked seizure. However, this patient’s seizure is likely caused by alcohol withdrawal. The patient’s symptoms should be treated with benzodiazepines, and a CT scan would not be the most appropriate next step unless a secondary insult were suspected.
wrongAnswers.E: Intubation (Choice E) would be appropriate in cases of obtundation, coma, severely depressed mental status, impaired ventilation, or impaired oxygenation. This patient is responding to verbal stimuli, breathing, and oxygenating well, making intubation inappropriate.

A CT scan of the head within 2 hours of arrival shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of these findings?

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
This patient is showing signs of brainstem dysfunction including altered level of consciousness, poor respiratory effort, posturing, and negative oculocephalic maneuver on examination. Dysfunction of the brainstem can also present with cranial nerve dysfunction, dizziness, vertigo, and gait instability, symptoms that the patient had been experiencing prior to this acute episode. The Babinski sign, or extensor plantar response, is an upper motor neuron sign that indicates damage to the corticospinal tract, a descending motor tract located in the central nervous system. The Babinski sign is present when the lateral part of the plantar surface of the foot is firmly stroked and the hallux extends (moves rostrally) while the other toes abduct. The doll’s eye (oculocephalic) maneuver refers to the brainstem reflex that occurs in normal adults in which the examiner moves the patient’s head, and the eyes move in the opposite direction to hold the patient’s gaze on an object. In a negative oculocephalic reflex, the patient’s eyes remain midline, which indicates severe brainstem dysfunction. The cause of

brainstem dysfunction in this patient is likely brainstem ischemia, which is often not disclosed on CT scan when acute. MRI is more sensitive for diagnosis. Patients with brainstem ischemia can have a stuttering course, which this patient experienced with mild intermittent symptoms prior to this presentation.

wrongAnswers.A: Brain stem demyelination (Choice A), such as in central pontine myelinolysis, can occur when there is rapid correction of hyponatremia. It typically involves demyelination of the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts resulting in acute, irreversible quadriparesis or quadriplegia, dysarthria, dysphagia, and/or confusion.
wrongAnswers.B: Brain stem hemorrhage (Choice B) can present with altered mental status, poor respiratory effort, and upper motor neuron findings such as in this patient. However, a CT scan of the head is sensitive for blood and would disclose hemorrhage as hyperdense material in the brainstem.
wrongAnswers.D: Cerebral hemispheric demyelination (Choice D) can occur as a chronic process such as in multiple sclerosis, which is an autoimmune demyelinating disease that presents with focal neurologic deficits separated in space and time.
wrongAnswers.E: Cerebral hemispheric hemorrhage (Choice E) would present with focal neurologic deficits, and CT scan of the head would show hyperdense material representing hemorrhage in the cerebrum.
wrongAnswers.F: Cerebral hemispheric ischemia (Choice F) may not be disclosed on noncontrast CT scan, but CT may show delayed signs of infarction. Large, vaso-occlusive infarctions with cerebral edema may be visible though, especially on CT angiography. Cerebral neurologic deficits would include focal hemibody paresis, neglect, aphasia, dysarthria, or visual field deficits. In contrast, patients with processes involving the brainstem typically present with global symptoms such as obtundation, respiratory depression, and posturing, such as in this patient.
wrongAnswers.G: Toxic-metabolic encephalopathy (Choice G) describes acute delirium, confusion, and global cerebral dysfunction in the absence of primary structural disease. It is typically diffuse and does not selectively abolish brainstem reflexes or cause the focal brainstem findings seen in this patient.

questions.subject: Otolaryngology

explanationPanel.correct: D. Rupture of the tympanic membrane
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: The tympanic membrane separates the external and middle ear and is important for the conductance and amplification of auditory vibrations. The tympanic membrane may be ruptured by blunt trauma to the external ear, by perforation with a cotton tipped swab, or by barotrauma, which most commonly occurs as a result of concussive blast injury (as in this case) or rapid ascent during diving. Patients may experience ipsilateral conductive hearing loss, ear pain, tinnitus, vertigo, or ipsilateral facial weakness caused by injury of the facial nerve. Patients should undergo an urgent examination to detect other cranial injuries, spinal injuries, or basilar skull fractures, along with evaluation for barotrauma involving other susceptible organ systems such as the respiratory system (pneumothorax) and the gastrointestinal tract (hollow viscus perforation). Initial management includes antibiotic ear drops, audiology, and referral to an otolaryngologist. Patients with severe conductive hearing loss often require surgical repair.

wrongAnswers.A: Fracture of the temporal bone (Choice A) is a type of basilar skull fracture that may lead to conductive hearing loss caused by injury to the ossicles or tympanic membrane. Basilar skull fracture is typically accompanied by other clinical signs and symptoms including hemotympanum, Battle sign, raccoon eyes, or cerebrospinal fluid otorrhea/rhinorrhea.
wrongAnswers.B: Injury to the air cells of the mastoid process (Choice B) typically occurs in the setting of mastoiditis. Mastoiditis presents with otalgia and retroauricular edema and erythema, and often follows a middle ear infection.
wrongAnswers.C: Pressure on the vestibulocochlear nerve (Choice C) presents with sensorineural hearing loss and is often accompanied by tinnitus, vertigo, and nystagmus.

Initial assessment and management should be directed toward detection of other blast-related injuries along with antibiotic ear drops and referral to an otolaryngologist.
explanationPanel.rule: Blast/barotrauma with ear pain, canal blood, and conductive hearing loss most directly indicates tympanic membrane rupture.
explanationPanel.trap: Basilar/temporal fracture has broader skull-base signs such as hemotympanum or Battle sign, not isolated blast TM findings.

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Febrile seizures are a common presentation in infants or young children. Simple and uncomplicated febrile seizures are generalized and defined as lasting less than 15 minutes and not recurring within a 24-hour period, whereas complex febrile seizures are focal, prolonged, and recurring. It is important to differentiate febrile seizures secondary to a viral illness from a bacterial central nervous system infection, which can also present with fever and seizure, but patients are typically ill-appearing and may have signs of meningismus. In patients with febrile seizures that have spontaneously resolved, active treatment with benzodiazepines is not necessary and the fever can be treated symptomatically with antipyretics (eg, acetaminophen). Most children who present with simple febrile seizures can be discharged safely as long as they have returned to baseline and parents are given anticipatory guidance and strict return precautions. Children with focal or prolonged seizures may require further observation, intervention, or diagnosis, especially if there is delayed recovery to baseline or a prolonged postictal phase.

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
The patient is presenting with signs and symptoms concerning for carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning and should be treated with hyperbaric oxygen therapy. CO has a significantly higher affinity for hemoglobin than oxygen and binds to available hemoglobin. On binding, CO displaces oxygen from heme, limiting total carrying capacity, and results in maintenance of hemoglobin in the relaxed form, with loss of cooperative binding. This results in systemic hypoxemia and tissue hypoxia. Risk factors include prolonged exposure to motor vehicle exhaust (as in operating an outboard motor for an extended period of time); exposure to byproducts of burning charcoal, gas, or petroleum (especially in poorly ventilated areas); or exposure to paint thinners that contain methylene chloride (which is metabolized to CO). Symptoms include headache, light-headedness, nausea, and altered mental status. Patients typically have a paradoxically normal peripheral oxygen saturation and may display tachycardia, tachypnea, and cherry-red skin on physical examination in the late stages of CO poisoning. Acute management involves removing the patient from the exposure and treatment with 100% supplemental oxygen to displace CO from hemoglobin. Severe cases and high-risk patients demonstrating any degree of neurologic deficit or significant end-organ dysfunction should be treated with

hyperbaric oxygen therapy. CO also binds cytochrome complexes and disrupts the electron transport chain; the resultant cellular dysfunction is best addressed with hyperbaric oxygen therapy.

wrongAnswers.A: Administration of ipecac (Choice A) is not recommended for treatment of CO poisoning. While historically ipecac was used to treat numerous types of oral toxin ingestions, it is no longer widely recommended because of limited established benefit and potential risk of harm. Similarly, gastric lavage (Choice C) was a common gastric decontamination procedure for oral toxic ingestions that is no longer widely recommended.
wrongAnswers.B: Administration of 0.9% saline and vitamin B (thiamine) (Choice B) would be an appropriate treatment for acute alcohol toxicity or withdrawal complicated by volume depletion, with thiamine given to prevent or treat Wernicke encephalopathy. wrongAnswers.C: Administration of ipecac (Choice A) is not recommended for treatment of CO poisoning. wrongAnswers.D: Hemodialysis (Choice D) can be utilized for toxin removal in acute overdose for specific agents. explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Symptoms of organophosphate poisoning are caused by increased concentrations of acetylcholine in the neuronal junction caused by the irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase. Organophosphates are present in pesticides and patients can be exposed through absorption, inhalation, or ingestion. Symptoms of cholinergic toxicity secondary to organophosphate poisoning included diarrhea, vomiting, excessive urination, lethargy, and altered mental status. Physical examination may demonstrate bradycardia, hypotension, miosis, increased salivation or tearing, diaphoresis, and evidence of bronchospasm. Muscle weakness and paralysis may be present, in addition to cardiac arrhythmias and respiratory failure. Long-term complications include neurocognitive deficits. Treatment consists of decontamination (eg, removal of contaminated clothing), fluid resuscitation, endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation if indicated, and administration of atropine. Atropine acts by competitively binding the acetylcholine receptors, which prevents the cholinergic effects of acetylcholine. Pralidoxime is used in the treatment of organophosphate poisoning and exerts its effects at the neuromuscular junction, where atropine is ineffective, by reactivating cholinesterase. Benzodiazepines may be administered if affected patients are

convulsing.

wrongAnswers.B: Administration of methylprednisolone (Choice B) is used in the treatment of allergic, autoimmune, and inflammatory conditions, such as asthma exacerbation, Crohn disease, and gout flares. It plays no role in the treatment of organophosphate poisoning.
wrongAnswers.C: Administration of morphine (Choice C) may improve pain and mildly improve shortness of breath. However, managing symptoms without treating the underlying pathology could lead to permanent injury, so administration of atropine is the most appropriate next step.
wrongAnswers.D: Administration of oxygen (Choice D) is useful in the treatment of hypoxia and may be beneficial in bronchoconstriction. However, it is not likely to completely alleviate this patient’s symptoms since the underlying mechanism is organophosphate poisoning, which requires treatment with atropine.
wrongAnswers.E: Administration of physostigmine (Choice E) would worsen his symptoms because physostigmine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. This would lead to further increases in the amount of acetylcholine available in the synapse and additional cholinergic signaling. It can be used, however, in the treatment of anticholinergic (eg, atropine) toxicity.
wrongAnswers.F: Administration of pralidoxime (Choice F) reactivates acetylcholinesterase and increases the amount of acetylcholine available to nicotinic receptors, where atropine does not bind. However, it should not be administered without concurrent atropine because it causes an initial decrease in acetylcholinesterase function.
wrongAnswers.G: Hemodialysis (Choice G) can be used to treat toxicities from agents such as tricyclic antidepressants, calcium channel blockers, methanol, and ethylene glycol. However, it is not a primary treatment option for organophosphate toxicity.

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: This patient presents with signs and symptoms of hypovolemic shock, most likely secondary to gastrointestinal fluid losses. Acute diarrheal illnesses are common in pediatric patients, and they are susceptible to developing clinically significant volume depletion. Loss of intravascular fluid results in decreased cardiac preload, with a consequent decrease in the cardiac output leading to a state of hypoperfusion. Pediatric patients typically present with lethargy. Signs of volume depletion include tachycardia, hypotension, a sunken anterior fontanelle, and dry mucous membranes. Despite the patient’s parents’ attempt to maintain hydration at home, administration of water alone is less effective than co-administration with a solute mixture, and losses from the gastrointestinal tract can quickly exceed the ability to replace them enterally. The patient requires emergent volume resuscitation and inpatient management.

wrongAnswers.B: Decreased venous tone (Choice B) is observed in distributive shock, which may be secondary to sepsis, anaphylaxis, or neurogenic causes. Patients with distributive shock who have maintained an adequate total body fluid status typically display peripheral edema, pulmonary crackles, and warm and flushed extremities as a result of capillary leak. Though this patient likely has an infection, results of physical examination and laboratory studies are evidence of a severely volume-depleted state which is the major contributor to her hypotension.
wrongAnswers.C: Increased pulmonary vascular resistance (Choice C) occurs in progressive pulmonary hypertension, acute pulmonary embolism, or congenital heart defects. The patient is not demonstrating findings consistent with right-sided heart failure, which would include peripheral edema, hepatomegaly, and jugular venous distention.
wrongAnswers.D: Increased stroke volume (Choice D) does not occur in hypovolemic shock; in fact, the decreased cardiac preload results in a decreased stroke volume. explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Vertebral artery dissection is the most common cause of stroke in young, healthy patients and can be caused by spontaneous dissection or can be secondary to trauma. explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Acute pericarditis is caused by an infectious, inflammatory, or malignant precipitant and presents as pleuritic chest pain that is exacerbated with lying down and alleviated by leaning forward. On examination, patients can have a friction rub on auscultation, which is

best heard with a patient leaning forward with the diaphragm of the stethoscope over the left sternal border. Chest x-ray would typically show no abnormalities, and ECG findings include diffuse (not focal) ST elevations and PR depressions. Echocardiography may also show a pericardial fluid collection. A moderate or large pericardial effusion can lead to complications such as cardiac tamponade, which presents with hypotension, jugular venous distention, distant heart sounds, and pulsus paradoxus. Treatment of pericarditis is typically supportive with colchicine and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications, such as ibuprofen.

wrongAnswers.A: Azithromycin (Choice A) is a typical treatment for community-acquired atypical pneumonia, usually caused by Chlamydia pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, or Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Atypical pneumonia is demonstrated on chest x-ray with bilateral patchy reticular or reticulonodular opacities. This patient has a normal chest x-ray and no cough, making pneumonia unlikely.
wrongAnswers.B: Heparin (Choice B) would be used in the treatment of pulmonary embolism, which can present with pleuritic chest pain and a normal chest x-ray. However, positional chest pain and a friction rub are more characteristic of pericarditis. In addition, this patient does not demonstrate any risk factors for pulmonary embolism and the ECG is more consistent with pericarditis. The ECG in a pulmonary embolus often shows sinus tachycardia and, if there is right heart strain, can exhibit right-axis deviation, S wave in lead I, Q wave in lead III, and inverted T wave in lead III. ST-segment elevation would not be expected.
wrongAnswers.D: Nitroglycerin (Choice D) can be used in the treatment of coronary artery disease and angina. Nitroglycerin is a potent venodilator, which decreases cardiac preload and myocardial oxygen demand, making it a first-line therapy in the treatment of angina pectoris.
wrongAnswers.E: Oxygen by face mask (Choice E) can be used in the treatment of spontaneous uncomplicated pneumothorax. Pneumothorax can appear on chest x-ray as radiolucent air and the absence of interstitial lung markings in the pleural space adjacent to the lung parenchyma.

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
This patient is likely experiencing acute heart failure from severe high blood pressure. Hypertensive emergency is defined as a blood pressure greater than 180/120 mm Hg with evidence of end-organ damage (eg, pulmonary edema and acute heart failure). The patient’s severe hypertension causes an acute increase in afterload that the heart is unable to overcome, and impaired forward flow of blood leads to congestion and increased hydrostatic pressure in the pulmonary vascular system and the systemic venous system. Cardiogenic pulmonary edema presents in patients with shortness of breath, tachypnea, hypoxia, and audible rales on examination. Intravenous antihypertensive medications should be used for the treatment of hypertensive emergency to appropriately decrease blood pressure and limit progression of end-organ damage. In acute heart failure and pulmonary edema, the blood pressure should be rapidly decreased using nitroglycerin, a potent vasodilator, to lower mean arterial pressure by decreasing

vascular resistance. Nitroglycerin, a venodilator, can also be used to shift fluid into capacitance vessels and lower preload. Positive pressure ventilation can also decrease alveolar and interstitial edema and drive fluid back into circulation.

wrongAnswers.A: Clopidogrel (Choice A) is an antiplatelet used in the prophylaxis and treatment of coronary artery disease and acute myocardial infarction. While acute myocardial infarction can also lead to acute heart failure and pulmonary edema, this patient’s heart failure is caused by hypertensive crisis. An ECG in a patient with acute myocardial infarction would typically show ST-segment elevation or depression, neither of which are seen in this example.
wrongAnswers.B: Furosemide (Choice B) is a diuretic that can be helpful in the treatment of chronic congestive heart failure which can lead to a hypervolemic state. While the patient presents with pulmonary edema, it is caused by acute increased hydrostatic pressure in the pulmonary vascular system and not by overall body hypervolemia. Furosemide would likely be used in caring for this patient; however, it would have a delayed effect as opposed to the immediate clinical effect of nitroglycerin, making it less appropriate as the best initial medication.
wrongAnswers.C: Heparin (Choice C) would be used in the treatment of pulmonary embolism, which typically presents with pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, and tachypnea. However, lungs would typically be clear on auscultation. This patient’s hypoxia and respiratory failure are caused by pulmonary congestion, demonstrated by rales on examination.
wrongAnswers.D: Milrinone (Choice D) would be used in the treatment of cardiogenic shock. While cardiogenic shock can also lead to pulmonary congestion, it is typically caused by left ventricular heart failure and decreased cardiac output, with hypotension and cool extremities on examination. This patient is presenting in hypertensive emergency.

The pupils are 6 mm and reactive to light. Abdominal examination shows decreased bowel sounds. This patient’s physical findings are most likely caused by which of the following substances?

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Diphenhydramine is a first-generation H1 receptor blocking agent that is commonly used for the treatment of allergies, insomnia, and motion sickness, with multiple off-label uses such as in the treatment of acute dystonic reactions and as an antiemetic. The main adverse effects of diphenhydramine arise from its action on multiple other receptor types, beyond the histamine receptor, notably anticholinergic and anti-α-adrenergic action. The effect on multiple receptors results in a constellation of symptoms such as dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, hallucinations, delirium, ataxia, mydriasis, tachycardia, flushed skin, visual disturbances (cycloplegia), hypotension, and sedation. Management of diphenhydramine overdoses and resultant toxidromes is focused on supportive care of a patient’s airway, breathing, and circulation while permitting metabolism of the drug. Patients should be placed on a cardiac monitor, administered IV fluids, and provided supplemental oxygen, as needed. Agitation or seizures should be treated with benzodiazepines. Administration of physostigmine can be considered for severe anticholinergic toxicity, as physostigmine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. This would lead to increased acetylcholine availability in the synapse resulting in counterbalancing cholinergic signaling.

wrongAnswers.A: Acetaminophen (Choice A) toxicity is characterized by acute liver failure. At high doses, saturation of metabolic pathways leads to excess acetaminophen being metabolized by cytochrome P450-mediated reactions to N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI), which has strong oxidizing properties and is hepatotoxic.
wrongAnswers.B: Alcohol (Choice B) is a central nervous system depressant and intoxication can cause slurred speech, emotional lability, behavioral disinhibition, ataxia, and memory lapses.
wrongAnswers.D: Marijuana (Choice D) is a hallucinogen that causes euphoria, anxiety, perception of slowed time, impaired judgement, increased appetite, and dry mouth. Tachycardia and hypertension may be present on examination. Conjunctival injection is common in marijuana intoxication. Patients with marijuana intoxication can also present with paranoid delusions, social withdrawal, and hallucinations.
wrongAnswers.E: Nicotine (Choice E) is a central nervous system stimulant found in tobacco. Nicotine toxicity includes agitation, tremors, palpitations, nausea, and vomiting, and in severe cases, seizures, and dysrhythmias.

explanationPanel.correct: C. Myocardial perfusion testing within 3 days
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Exertional chest pain accompanied by shortness of breath that improves with rest is suggestive of stable angina pectoris, caused by cardiac ischemia from insufficient perfusion during exertion through narrowed atherosclerotic coronary arteries. This patient presents with symptoms consistent with unstable angina, defined by angina symptoms

that are new, occur at rest, or are worsening in severity. Unstable angina is a type of acute coronary syndrome, which requires urgent diagnostic workup including serial ECGs, troponin testing, cardiology consultation, and myocardial perfusion testing, stress testing, or cardiac catheterization. Nitroglycerin is a potent venodilator that decreases cardiac preload and myocardial oxygen demand, making it a first-line therapy in the treatment of angina pectoris along with aspirin, which inhibits platelet aggregation. Patients with unstable angina are stratified on the basis of the Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) score, which assists in identifying the need for therapeutic anticoagulation and coronary angiography. In this patient with improving chest pain, a normal ECG, and serial troponin concentrations within the reference range, the most appropriate next step in management is urgent myocardial perfusion testing.

wrongAnswers.A: CT scan of the chest with pulmonary embolism protocol (Choice A) would not be appropriate diagnostic workup in this patient. Pulmonary embolism typically presents with pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxia, tachypnea, hemoptysis, or syncope. This patient is presenting with chest pain with similar episodes during exertion that is relieved with aspirin, nitroglycerin, and morphine, which is more consistent with anginal chest pain.
wrongAnswers.B: Emergent cardiac catheterization (Choice B) would be appropriate in cases of acute myocardial infarction, which would present similarly with anginal chest pain but would have ECG changes showing ST-segment elevation and increased concentrations of serum troponin. This patient’s diagnostic work-up shows no abnormalities, making acute myocardial infarction unlikely. This patient may require cardiac catheterization because his TIMI score is high; however, it (or a noninvasive stress test) should occur urgently within 3 days, as opposed to emergently.

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Infection is the most likely precipitant of this patient’s acute chest syndrome (ACS). ACS

occurs as a result of vaso-occlusion within the pulmonary microvasculature and is diagnosed in patients with sickle cell disease (SCD) who present with a new pulmonary infiltrate in the setting of fever or other new respiratory symptoms, including cough, shortness of breath, increased work of breathing, tachypnea, or hypoxemia. While ACS is a distinct clinical syndrome, it is commonly precipitated by another illness such as bacterial or viral pneumonia, asthma exacerbation with hypoventilation, or fat emboli, among others. It is both impractical and nearly impossible to distinguish ACS from pneumonia, so nearly all patients receive antibiotics to treat bacterial pneumonia. Additionally, the use of either simple transfusion or exchange transfusion may be a component of therapy. Further treatment involves maintaining normoxia with supplemental oxygen or the use of noninvasive positive pressure ventilation, judicious use of fluids, and aggressive pulmonary hygiene measures, including the use of an incentive spirometer. Patients with a pulmonary embolism should be placed on full anticoagulation while all others should receive prophylaxis against venous thromboembolism. Pain should be managed aggressively.

wrongAnswers.B: Embolism (Choice B) should always be considered in patients with ACS, but thrombi found within the pulmonary vasculature are more likely to form in situ rather than represent emboli from the veins of the lower extremities. wrongAnswers.C: Hypoventilation (Choice C) can precipitate ACS, but this patient’s prodrome with cough and shortness of breath is more suggestive of pneumonia than hypoventilation in isolation. explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common bacterial cause of community-acquired pneumonia and has an increased prevalence in patients with a history of immunocompromise, such as HIV, multiple myeloma, or following solid organ transplant. Typical signs and symptoms of pneumococcal pneumonia include fever, chills, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, dyspnea, productive cough, rales, decreased breath sounds, increased tactile fremitus, and pleuritic chest pain. Plain film x-ray commonly discloses a lobar pneumonia or, less commonly, bronchopneumonia. The diagnosis may be supported by sputum culture with the presence of gram-positive diplococci in chains. Patients with evidence of unstable vital signs should undergo blood culture to evaluate for possible bacteremia. Therapy includes support of vitals as well as empiric antibiotic therapy either with a third-generation cephalosporin and macrolide or with fluoroquinolones. While pneumococcal pneumonia remains the leading cause of

community-acquired pneumonia, prophylaxis with pneumococcal vaccines has led to a decline in its incidence over recent decades.

wrongAnswers.A: Adenovirus (Choice A) is a cause of viral pneumonia and may lead to severe infections in patients who are immunocompromised. However, this patient’s fever and the presence of gram-positive diplococci on sputum culture are suggestive of pneumococcal pneumonia.
wrongAnswers.B: Coxsackievirus (Choice B) is an RNA enterovirus that is transmitted via oral secretions or feces. Coxsackievirus group A causes hand, foot, and mouth disease and herpangina. Coxsackievirus group B may cause myocarditis and pericarditis.
wrongAnswers.C: Haemophilus influenza (Choice C) is an encapsulated gram-negative bacillus that is a common cause of pneumonia in adults. However, it is less common in comparison to S. pneumoniae (a gram-positive coccus).
wrongAnswers.D: Klebsiella pneumoniae (Choice D) is a gram-negative bacillus that classically causes hospital-acquired pneumonia. It is less frequently a cause of community-acquired pneumonia.
wrongAnswers.E: Legionella pneumophila (Choice E) is a gram-negative bacillus that is transmitted through aerosols from water sources and causes atypical pneumonia that appears as diffuse, patchy alveolar and interstitial opacities or as a lobar consolidation. It can be associated with hyponatremia.
wrongAnswers.F: Moraxella catarrhalis (Choice F) is a gram-negative diplococcus that is a rare cause of pneumonia in immunocompromised adults. It typically causes bacterial rhinosinusitis and has been implicated in exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in adults.
wrongAnswers.H: Pneumocystis jirovecii (Choice H) is a yeast-like fungus which causes pneumocystis pneumonia in patients who are immunocompromised. Chest imaging typically shows diffuse, bilateral perihilar infiltrates. Pneumocystis pneumonia is less common than pneumococcal pneumonia and does not produce gram-positive diplococci on sputum Gram stain.
wrongAnswers.I: Staphylococcal (Choice I) pneumonia typically presents as a lobar pneumonia that occurs in elderly adults following a preceding viral infection.

She says the chest pain is worse when she takes a deep breath. During the past week, she has had pain and swelling of her left leg. She does not use oral contraceptives. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 3 years. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 130/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 140/85 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. Lungs are clear to auscultation. A urine pregnancy test is negative. An ECG is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
questions.subject: Pulmonology

explanationPanel.correct: B. CT angiography of the chest
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: CT angiography of the chest is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis. This young patient with new-onset exertional dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, recent lower extremity swelling suggestive of deep venous thrombosis (DVT), and tachycardia most likely has a pulmonary embolism (PE). The Wells score for pulmonary embolism can be a helpful tool in determining the likelihood of a DVT or PE and directs the most appropriate diagnostic step, which can include a D-dimer or image-based test such as CT angiography. In patients with a low pretest probability, a negative D-dimer effectively rules out a PE. In those with a higher score, the most appropriate diagnostic test is CT angiography, which is a CT scan with iodinated contrast timed to evaluate the pulmonary arteries. Pregnant patients or those with contraindications to CT scans or contrast can undergo ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scans, although this imaging modality is not universally available. Pulmonary emboli can be found in the main pulmonary, segmental, or subsegmental arteries and appear as filling defects on imaging. For patients without evidence of cardiogenic shock, treatment is systemic anticoagulation, which can be accomplished with warfarin, low-molecular-weight heparin, or with direct oral anticoagulants. ECG findings in PE include sinus tachycardia, right-axis deviation, right bundle branch block, an S-wave in lead I, a Q wave in lead III, and an inverted T wave in lead III.

wrongAnswers.A: Measurement of serum troponin I (Choice A) is unlikely to lead to a diagnosis in this case. Troponin is a cardiac biomarker that can occasionally be increased in cases of pulmonary embolism with associated right heart strain or failure, but it does not confirm the diagnosis.
wrongAnswers.C: D-dimer assay (Choice C) is used to rule out PE in patients with a low to intermediate probability of PE, but this patient has a high probability of PE and should proceed directly to CT angiography.
wrongAnswers.D: Echocardiography (Choice D) is indicated if there is evidence of shock secondary to right ventricular failure. Large pulmonary emboli can cause obstructive shock and right ventricular failure, which is demonstrated on echocardiography by right ventricular dilation or hypokinesis or bowing of the interventricular septum into the left ventricle.
wrongAnswers.E: Measurement of brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) (Choice E) is appropriate for patients who are suspected to have acute decompensated heart failure. BNP is released by the ventricles in response to stretch from increased volume or pressure. It may be increased in cases of PE with shock but is also nonspecific.

In patients with a high probability of PE, CT angiography is the most appropriate next diagnostic step. In patients who are stable without evidence of shock, systemic anticoagulation should be started immediately.

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Intravenous administration of alteplase is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient with a confirmed pulmonary embolism and evidence of obstructive shock. Large pulmonary emboli (PE) increase the resistance within the pulmonary arterial circuit and place undue strain on the right ventricle. When this pulmonary resistance exceeds the capability of the right ventricle to maintain forward cardiac output, patients can develop signs and symptoms of shock. Common findings include hypoxemia, tachycardia, hypotension, and altered mental status. Laboratory markers may demonstrate increased brain natriuretic peptide and increased troponin concentrations. Bedside echocardiography is a useful tool and may show a dilated and hypokinetic right ventricle with bowing of the interventricular septum into the left ventricle. The decision to give thrombolytics such as alteplase should weigh the risks for bleeding with the risk for death from a PE. In instances of shock, the risk for death from a PE nearly always outweighs the risk for bleeding; thus, this patient should be given alteplase as soon as possible. Following thrombolysis, patients should be placed on systemic anticoagulation with intravenous unfractionated heparin.

wrongAnswers.B: Intravenous administration of unfractionated heparin (Choice B) is one treatment option for patients with low- or intermediate-risk PE without evidence of shock. This patient requires thrombolytics; systemic anticoagulation should be resumed after administration of alteplase. Similarly, oral administration of warfarin (Choice C) is another option for long-term treatment of PE, but newer agents such as direct oral anticoagulants or low-molecular-weight heparin are typically preferred given their ease of dosing and efficacy. Shock is a primary indication for the use of thrombolytics, which should be given before systemic anticoagulants.

wrongAnswers.E: Subcutaneous administration of enoxaparin (Choice E), also known as low-molecular-weight heparin, is a reasonable treatment strategy to prevent the development of DVT and PE but is not used for patients with evidence of shock.

questions.explanation: Intravenous administration of alteplase is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient with a confirmed pulmonary embolism and evidence of obstructive shock. Large pulmonary emboli (PE) increase the resistance within the pulmonary arterial circuit and place undue strain on the right ventricle. When this pulmonary resistance exceeds the capability of the right ventricle to maintain forward cardiac output, patients can develop signs and symptoms of shock. Common findings include hypoxemia, tachycardia, hypotension, and altered mental status. Laboratory markers may demonstrate increased brain natriuretic peptide and increased troponin concentrations. Bedside echocardiography is a useful tool and may show a dilated and hypokinetic right ventricle with bowing of the interventricular septum into the left ventricle. The decision to give thrombolytics such as alteplase should weigh the risks for bleeding with the risk for death from a PE. In instances of shock, the risk for death from a PE nearly always outweighs the risk for bleeding; thus, this patient should be given alteplase as soon as possible. Following thrombolysis, patients should be placed on systemic anticoagulation with intravenous unfractionated heparin. Patients with large pulmonary emboli leading to right ventricular failure and obstructive shock should receive thrombolytic agents such as alteplase. explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Admission to the hospital for observation is the most appropriate management for this young girl who recently suffered a nonfatal drowning incident. Unexpected submersion in water leads to reflexive breath holding followed by air hunger and an eventual reflexive inspiratory effort. This leads to hypoxia through either aspiration of water or laryngospasm when water contacts the vocal cords. Prolonged hypoxemia leads to end-organ dysfunction including acidosis, hypoxic brain injury, and cardiac arrhythmias. Exposure of the alveoli to water can lead to the development of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), which appears on chest imaging as noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. ARDS can develop immediately after injury or slowly over many hours and can be rapidly fatal. In general, all nonfatal drowning victims with any degree of hypoxia, respiratory distress, or infiltrates on imaging should be hospitalized to monitor for the evidence of the development of ARDS and complications of drowning.

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Asthma is characterized by reversible obstruction of the bronchi secondary to hyperreactivity and airway inflammation. Patients present with episodes of wheezing, dry cough, and dyspnea. The management of asthma exacerbations is directed toward maintaining oxygenation, rapidly reversing bronchospasm, and alleviating symptoms of respiratory distress. Short-acting inhaled β-adrenergic agonists, such as albuterol, are firstline for the management of asthma exacerbations. Patients who do not respond to initial therapy with metered-dose inhalers may benefit from nebulizer treatment. Anticholinergics, steroids, and magnesium are also often employed in moderate to severe exacerbations.

wrongAnswers.A: Inhaled fluticasone (Choice A) is useful as part of the daily management of persistent asthma and for the prevention of acute asthma exacerbations. However, it is not as rapidly effective as inhaled/nebulized short-acting β-adrenergic agonists for acute bronchospasm.
wrongAnswers.C: Magnesium sulfate (Choice C) is a bronchodilator that is useful for the management of asthma exacerbations that do not respond to initial treatment with inhaled β-adrenergic agonists.
wrongAnswers.D: Intravenous methylprednisolone (Choice D) is useful for the treatment of acute asthma exacerbation and leads to an improvement in symptoms and decreased rates of recurrent exacerbations. However, the onset of action of systemic glucocorticoids typically requires several hours. This patient’s acute respiratory distress should first be addressed with inhaled β-adrenergic agonists.
wrongAnswers.E: Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation (Choice E) may be necessary for patients with severe asthma exacerbations that are nonresponsive to inhaled β-adrenergic agonist therapy and are accompanied by significant oxygen desaturation, increased work of breathing, hypercapnia, or respiratory distress.

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Tension pneumothorax can be a complication of a penetrating thoracic trauma and occurs when air is able to enter the pleural space but is prevented from exiting. Increasing amounts of trapped air in the pleural space compress the lung parenchyma, creating an inability for the lung to expand and causing it to collapse. As the pneumothorax progresses and continues to increase in size, it can result in tracheal and/or mediastinal deviation away from the affected hemithorax. It can result in decreased venous return to the heart, which manifests with hypotension and obstructive shock. Tension pneumothorax is characterized by absent breath sounds and hyperresonance to percussion caused by the increased air in the intrathoracic space displacing normal lung parenchyma. In cases of acute tension pneumothorax, evacuating the accumulated air via needle decompression and aspiration permits expansion of the lung and eliminates tension on the mediastinal structures, resolving obstructive shock. Immediate needle decompression is followed by tube thoracostomy, which promotes expansion of the lung, prevents reaccumulation of air, and promotes healing of the pleural defect.

wrongAnswers.A: Intravenous administration of 0.9% saline (Choice A) can be helpful for patients with hypotension secondary to distributive shock such as anaphylaxis or sepsis. This patient’s tension pneumothorax is causing an obstructive shock, and fluid administration would not resolve the deficit.
wrongAnswers.C: Pericardial window (Choice C) or pericardiocentesis (Choice D) would be indicated in cases of traumatic pericardial effusion causing cardiac tamponade. Tamponade presents with hypotension, jugular venous distention, distant heart sounds, and pulsus paradoxus. This patient has decreased breath sounds, tachypnea, and hypoxia, making pneumothorax more likely.
wrongAnswers.D: Pericardial window (Choice C) or pericardiocentesis (Choice D) would be indicated in cases of traumatic pericardial effusion causing cardiac tamponade. Tamponade presents with hypotension, jugular venous distention, distant heart sounds, and pulsus paradoxus. This patient has decreased breath sounds, tachypnea, and hypoxia, making pneumothorax more likely.
wrongAnswers.E: Thoracotomy (Choice E) is an invasive procedure that allows for control of thoracic hemorrhage, decompression of cardiac tamponade, or management of aortic or pulmonary hemorrhage. It can be indicated in cases of penetrating trauma with hemodynamic instability despite appropriate management, or of pulselessness and receiving CPR for less than 15 minutes with witnessed previous signs of life. This patient’s hemodynamic instability is likely caused by tension pneumothorax, which should be managed by needle decompression and tube thoracostomy, not thoracotomy.
wrongAnswers.F: Tube thoracostomy (Choice F) typically follows needle decompression, which is an emergent and rapid maneuver that can help temporize the patient in preparation for eventual tube thoracostomy. Tube thoracostomy should be done under sterile conditions and requires several minutes.

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Common bile duct obstruction is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms. The patient’s increased concentrations of lipase and amylase in the setting of typical epigastric pain are most consistent with pancreatitis, and the concurrent presence of direct hyperbilirubinemia, transaminitis, and fever are concerning for concomitant early cholangitis. While there are numerous causes of pancreatitis, the most common causes include gallstones and heavy alcohol consumption. Gallstones that pass out of the gallbladder through the cystic duct eventually reach the common bile duct (CBD). The main pancreatic duct also connects to the CBD, which is a conduit for pancreatic enzymes to reach the duodenum. If gallstones become lodged in the distal aspect of the CBD, obstruction of pancreatic flow can lead to release and activation of pancreatic

enzymes within the pancreas, which causes substantial inflammation and pain. Additionally, as the flow of bile toward the duodenum is obstructed, patients can develop hyperbilirubinemia and increased liver enzymes. This can predispose to cholangitis, which is an ascending bacterial infection of the biliary tree. Treatment for gallstone pancreatitis is either cholecystectomy with intraoperative cholangiography or, in most cases, endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) to retrieve the obstructing gallstone. While awaiting procedural intervention, patients should be treated with intravenous fluids, narcotic pain medications, and antibiotics if there is suspicion for biliary tree infection.

wrongAnswers.A: Alcohol-induced pancreatitis (Choice A) is a common cause of pancreatitis, but this patient with a history of hyperlipidemia, increased bilirubin, and increased liver-associated enzymes is more likely to have gallstone pancreatitis. Increased direct bilirubin would not be classic if alcohol was the primary cause.
wrongAnswers.B: Cholecystitis (Choice B) is caused by obstruction of the cystic duct and presents with right upper quadrant pain, fever, and evidence of gallbladder inflammation on ultrasonography. It does not result in increased liver-associated enzymes.
wrongAnswers.D: Drug-induced hepatic dysfunction (Choice D) can either be idiosyncratic or dose-dependent, as in the case of acetaminophen overdose. It may present with increased concentrations of ALT, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin, but it requires a compatible history of drug exposure, which is absent in this case.
wrongAnswers.E: Duodenal ulceration (Choice E) may present with epigastric pain and may cause gastrointestinal bleeding with subsequent melena, but it does not cause an increase in liver enzymes.

Treatment is intravenous fluids, pain control, and ERCP to remove the obstructing gallstone. Cholecystectomy should be performed in all patients when safe to do so.

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: CT angiography is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis. This patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), recent weight loss, and postprandial abdominal pain most likely has nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia. Mesenteric ischemia can occur secondary to thrombosis of the mesenteric artery or can result from low-flow cardiac states leading to intestinal hypoperfusion. The blood supply to the intestines is primarily derived from the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) and inferior mesenteric artery (IMA). Following a meal, the blood flow to the intestines increases to aid in the digestive process. In nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia, constriction of the mesenteric artery in combination with a decreased cardiac output leads to a supply–demand mismatch and subsequent intestinal ischemia. This is often experienced as postprandial pain which may make some patients avoid eating altogether, thereby leading to weight loss. The diagnosis is made by CT angiography, which shows narrowing of the mesenteric vessels and their branches. When the condition is secondary to HFrEF, therapy is aimed at improving cardiac function.

wrongAnswers.A: Abdominal ultrasonography (Choice A) can be used to evaluate the abdominal aorta and flow through its main branches, which include the SMA, IMA, and celiac trunk, but advanced cross-sectional imaging with CT angiography is more sensitive and specific for mesenteric ischemia.
wrongAnswers.B: Barium enema (Choice B) is used infrequently in current clinical practice, but it can occasionally help to diagnose malrotation or volvulus. It is not helpful in the diagnosis of mesenteric ischemia.
wrongAnswers.D: Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (Choice D) is used to evaluate the esophagus, stomach, and the duodenum and can diagnose conditions such as peptic ulcer disease, esophagitis, or esophageal cancer among others. This patient does not have features suggestive of these disease processes.
wrongAnswers.E: Upper gastrointestinal series with small bowel follow through (Choice E) is sometimes used to evaluate for the presence of small bowel obstruction, but CT imaging with contrast is more sensitive for the diagnosis. Patients usually present with nausea, vomiting, and failure to pass flatus. This patient’s presentation is not consistent with this diagnosis.

In the latter case, low-flow cardiac states in conjunction with mesenteric artery spasm or narrowing lead to a supply–demand mismatch in the postprandial period. This leads to postprandial abdominal pain and gradual weight loss. Diagnosis is made by CT angiography to visualize the mesenteric vessels and their branches.

The diagnosis is made by CT angiography, which shows narrowing of the mesenteric vessels and their branches. When the condition is secondary to HFrEF, therapy is aimed at improving cardiac function. Mesenteric ischemia can be occlusive or nonocclusive. In the latter case, low-flow cardiac states in conjunction with mesenteric artery spasm or narrowing lead to a supply–demand mismatch in the postprandial period. explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Upper endoscopy is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis in this patient with signs and symptoms of upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB). Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding is often separated into upper and lower GI bleeding. Patients with UGIB often present with dizziness or light-headedness, nausea, epigastric pain, and melena. Occasionally, as in the case of variceal bleeding, hematemesis may accompany these symptoms. Laboratory findings may show an increased blood urea nitrogen concentration, but the decrease in hemoglobin concentration often lags behind clinically significant bleeding. Treatment should initially focus on resuscitation with crystalloids and erythrocyte transfusion as needed. All patients are started on an intravenous proton pump inhibitor, and patients with cirrhosis and suspected variceal bleeding should receive octreotide and antibiotics. Major causes of UGIB aside from esophageal varices include Mallory-Weiss tear, peptic ulcer disease, gastritis, esophagitis, and angiodysplasia. Rare causes include Dieulafoy lesion, gastric antral vascular ectasia, and aortoenteric fistula. After patients have been stabilized, upper endoscopy should be performed both to determine the cause of bleeding and to intervene on any lesions that are amenable to treatment, such as bleeding ulcers or visibly bleeding blood vessels.

wrongAnswers.A: CT scan of the abdomen (Choice A) is insensitive for evaluating the cause of gastrointestinal bleeding. Resuscitation followed by endoscopy should generally be performed first. wrongAnswers.B: Colonoscopy (Choice B) is the intervention of choice when patients are suspected of having a source of lower GI bleeding such as diverticulosis or angiodysplasia, which often presents with hematochezia rather than melena.
wrongAnswers.D: Celiac angiography (Choice D) is not the correct answer. wrongAnswers.E: Exploratory operation (Choice E) is indicated in patients who develop perforated bowel. While this can occur in the setting of gastric or duodenal ulcers, it is rare, and patients often have peritoneal signs on examination and evidence of sepsis, which this patient lacks.

explanationPanel.correct: C. Consultation with surgery for appendectomy
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Appendicitis is acute inflammation of the appendix and usually results from appendiceal obstruction by a fecalith or by lymphoid hyperplasia. Appendiceal obstruction leads to bacterial proliferation within the lumen and wall of the appendix, eventually leading to inflammation, infection, appendiceal necrosis, and perforation. Acute appendicitis typically presents with abdominal pain that is often periumbilical at onset and which may later migrate to the right lower quadrant, along with leukocytosis and tenderness to palpation. Patients often develop fever and may also experience nausea and anorexia. Other genitourinary, vascular, musculoskeletal, and gastrointestinal mimics should be excluded. The diagnosis can be confirmed with CT scan, MRI, or ultrasonography. Appendectomy is indicated to prevent appendiceal rupture, which can lead to peritonitis or an intra-abdominal abscess. In equivocal cases with negative imaging, serial abdominal examinations are often performed to evaluate for the development of the condition.

wrongAnswers.A: Admission for colonoscopy (Choice A) will not be useful for the diagnosis of acute appendicitis. Colonoscopy is useful for the detection of colon carcinoma, arteriovenous malformation, polyp, or stricture.
wrongAnswers.B: Consultation with gynecology for diagnostic laparoscopy (Choice B) is useful for the management of ovarian torsion or endometriosis but is not necessary for this patient. Ovarian torsion causes lower abdominal or pelvic pain but does not present with pain that migrates from the umbilicus to the right lower quadrant. Ovarian torsion can be identified by decreased flow on pelvic Doppler ultrasonography.
wrongAnswers.D: Discharge after administration of ceftriaxone and azithromycin (Choice D) is appropriate for the treatment of gonorrhea and chlamydia. This patient’s history of migratory right lower quadrant pain is more suggestive of appendicitis.
wrongAnswers.E: Discharge with a prescription for oral ciprofloxacin and metronidazole (Choice E) remains a controversial therapeutic strategy for acute appendicitis and is not currently the standard of care. While there is evidence that nonoperative management of acute appendicitis with antibiotics may be effective for some patients, predicting the response to therapy is difficult, and patients managed medically may have a higher rate of recurrent appendicitis.

explanationPanel.correct: C. Insertion of a nasogastric tube
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Bowel obstruction is the most likely diagnosis in a patient with previous abdominal surgery presenting with abdominal pain and obstipation. Obstruction of the bowel occurs from partial or complete blockage of the bowel lumen and typically presents with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Partial obstruction allows a degree of continued flatus with diminished stooling, and complete obstruction will result in obstipation (no passage of stool or flatus). Obstruction has many potential causes, although the most common are postsurgical peritoneal adhesions and hernias. On physical examination, patients typically present with abdominal tenderness, distention, tympany to percussion, and borborygmi (high-pitched, hyperactive bowel sounds). Potential complications include bowel rupture and necrosis, which can result in sudden-onset peritoneal signs such as rebound tenderness and guarding. X-ray of the abdomen typically discloses multiple air-fluid levels in the setting of dilated bowel loops. Management requires bowel rest, insertion of a nasogastric tube for decompression, and intravenous hydration followed by surgical intervention if the obstruction does not autoreduce. Partial obstruction may resolve with monitoring, supportive care, and bowel rest, whereas complete obstruction

or any complicated partial obstruction generally requires management through exploratory laparotomy.

wrongAnswers.A: Complete blood count (Choice A) can be done as part of routine blood work prior to possible surgery or hospitalization, but it would not change or assist in the management.
wrongAnswers.B: Exploratory laparotomy (Choice B) can be done for obstruction that does not autoreduce with bowel rest and decompression but would not be appropriate prior to insertion of a nasogastric tube for management. Surgery is also indicated in cases of perforation or necrosis, but this patient does not show any signs of peritonitis or guarding suggestive of these complications.
wrongAnswers.D: Intravenous antibiotic therapy (Choice D) would be indicated in cases of bowel perforation, sepsis, or necrosis, but this patient does not show any signs of peritonitis or guarding suggestive of these complications. Antibiotics are not routinely indicated in the management of bowel obstruction.
wrongAnswers.E: Manual disimpaction (Choice E) can be helpful in cases of constipation and obstructing rectal stool burden. However, this patient’s obstipation is caused by an intraperitoneal process, not constipation.
