explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Exploratory laparotomy involves the surgical evaluation of the peritoneal cavity and is commonly employed in the diagnosis and management of abdominal trauma, bowel obstruction, peritonitis, and undifferentiated cases of acute abdomen. In penetrating abdominal trauma, evaluation of the depth of the wound tract is quickly done to determine whether it has violated the peritoneum. Gunshot wounds are particularly high-energy and can cause severe intra-abdominal injury including hemorrhage and viscus perforation. Laparotomy of the abdomen is indicated for hemodynamically unstable patients (eg, tachycardia and hypotension) presenting after penetrating abdominal trauma because it permits the control of hemorrhage and the repair of identified injuries. In stable cases, imaging precedes surgical intervention.

wrongAnswers.A: Observation (Choice A) could potentially be appropriate for a patient who is hemodynamically stable and with a superficially penetrating wound not violating the peritoneum. It would be inappropriate in this borderline unstable patient with a severe penetrating wound with likely intra-abdominal injury.
wrongAnswers.B: Arteriography (Choice B) has been used for evaluation of arterial anatomy and pathology. However, CT angiography has primarily taken over the role of diagnosis in the traumatic setting. In a hemodynamically unstable patient, however, laparotomy is the most appropriate next step.
wrongAnswers.C: Contrast study of the wound tract (Choice C) would not be an appropriate imaging study in an acute traumatic setting in a hemodynamically unstable patient. Contrast study of tracts can be used to evaluate patency and location of things like gastrostomy tubes, cholecystostomy tubes, and jejunostomy tubes.
wrongAnswers.D: CT scan of the abdomen (Choice D) would be helpful in diagnosing other traumatic injuries such as liver or splenic lacerations, duodenal hematoma, bowel perforation, or retroperitoneal hematoma. However, for patients who are hemodynamically unstable, a CT scan may delay diagnosis and prompt management of intra-abdominal injuries.
wrongAnswers.E: Intravenous pyelography (Choice E) involves the intravenous injection of radio-opaque contrast to visualize the renal collecting system, ureters, and bladder under fluoroscopy. This allows for the investigation of suspected urinary tract anatomic abnormalities, malignancies, and strictures.
wrongAnswers.F: Laparoscopy (Choice F) would be indicated in abdominal trauma in stable patients with equivocal findings on CT scan or diagnostic uncertainty.
wrongAnswers.H: Peritoneal lavage (Choice H) is used for the evaluation of hemoperitoneum in abdominal injury. While it has mostly been replaced by evaluation with ultrasonography, CT scan, or laparoscopy, it may be useful in situations with equivocal results or in low-resource settings.
wrongAnswers.I: Ultrasonography of the abdomen (Choice I) has a role in evaluating for the presence of intra-abdominal hemorrhage in hemodynamically unstable patients with blunt trauma. For an unstable patient with a penetrating abdominal gunshot wound and peritoneal violation, emergent laparotomy is required.

explanationPanel.correct: D. Packed red blood cell transfusion
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Packed red blood cell transfusion is the most appropriate next step in management for this patient with evidence of hemorrhagic shock secondary to gastrointestinal (GI) hemorrhage despite early and appropriate resuscitation with crystalloids. Hemorrhagic shock can occasionally occur in the setting of GI bleeding and manifests as hypotension, tachycardia, and evidence of end-organ damage, including increased lactate or serum creatinine concentrations or altered mental status. In acute GI bleeding, a measured drop

in the hemoglobin concentration often lags behind clinically significant blood loss, so all patients who remain clinically unstable or have persistent laboratory evidence of inadequate perfusion and oxygenation (eg, increased lactate) despite adequate resuscitation with crystalloids should receive packed red blood cells (pRBCs). In stable patients with GI bleeding, the threshold for transfusion of pRBCs should be when the hemoglobin drops below 7 g/dL (70 g/L).

wrongAnswers.B: Dopamine infusion (Choice B) is sometimes an appropriate intervention for patients with cardiogenic shock but would be inappropriate for a patient with hemorrhagic shock. Similarly, norepinephrine infusion (Choice C) is incorrect because this patient requires the additional oxygen-carrying capacity of red blood cells, not vasopressors.

yp p y g ureter (ureterolithiasis) includes severe, intermittent, sharp flank pain with either gross or microscopic hematuria, leukocytosis, and occasionally evidence of a concomitant urinary tract infection. explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Testicular torsion is caused by rotation of the testes around the spermatic cord. Compression of the blood vessel supply leads to edema, ischemia, and subsequent necrosis. It classically presents with acute testicular pain, tenderness to palpation, scrotal swelling, and a negative cremasteric reflex. The patient may also develop nausea and emesis and/or lower abdominal pain prior to the onset of scrotal pain. Physical examination may show a high-riding testis that is oriented transversely with surrounding erythema. Testicular torsion is typically a clinical diagnosis, although ultrasonography can be used for further evaluation if the diagnosis is unclear. Ultrasonography will demonstrate diminished or absent blood flow to the testes. Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency and requires surgical evaluation when the diagnosis is suspected. Surgery will allow for detorsion of the testes and orchiopexy (testicular fixation) of both testes to prevent recurrent torsion.

explanationPanel.correct: C. Measurement of serum β-hCG concentration
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Women of reproductive age presenting for care because of pelvic pain or abdominal cramping should be evaluated for pregnancy with a measurement of serum β-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) concentration. Pregnancy is suspected when there is a missed or delayed menstrual period. Ectopic pregnancy is an abnormal pregnancy in which the fertilized ovum implants in the fallopian tube (most common), on the ovary, within the peritoneal cavity, or in any nonendometrial location. It often causes symptoms early in pregnancy because of the restricted area for fetal development and commonly presents with lower abdominal or pelvic pain and vaginal bleeding. Physical examination may disclose adnexal tenderness on the side of implantation. β-hCG is produced by the placenta, is undetectable in the serum of nonpregnant patients, and doubles approximately every 48 hours during an early normal pregnancy. β-hCG concentrations do not increase as expected in ectopic pregnancy, often lagging the normal expected doubling. An ectopic pregnancy is not viable. Treatment of an ectopic pregnancy can be medical, using methotrexate for small, early pregnancies, but may require salpingectomy or evacuation with laparoscopy for larger pregnancies or in cases of medical treatment failure. Complications of ectopic pregnancy include rupture, bleeding, and hemoperitoneum.

She says she felt well until this morning. One week ago, she had an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery of a female newborn at term. Her postpartum vaginal bleeding had been decreasing daily until today, when she began passing some blood clots and soaking through a sanitary pad every 2 hours. Her current temperature is 37.9°C (100.3°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 102/66 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 99%. On examination, the abdomen is soft and diffusely tender to palpation of the lower quadrants; there is no rebound tenderness or guarding. The uterine fundus is firm, tender, and palpable inferior to the umbilicus. Her hematocrit is 29% and leukocyte count is 15,200/mm³ (15.2 × 10⁹/L). explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Postpartum hemorrhage is a relatively common complication of childbirth. wrongAnswers.B: Methotrexate therapy (Choice B) is used in the treatment of gestational trophoblastic disease and ectopic pregnancy. wrongAnswers.C: Methylprednisolone therapy (Choice C) is used to treat a variety of allergic, inflammatory, and autoimmune disorders. However, it plays no role in the treatment of secondary postpartum hemorrhage or retained products of conception.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 35-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of progressive redness and swelling of his right knee for the past 3 days. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 134/74 mm Hg. Examination shows a 1.5 × 3-cm area of swelling and fluctuance over the anterior aspect of the right knee. A photograph is shown. Range of motion of the knee is full. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

explanationPanel.correct: B. Incision and drainage of the affected area
explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
Abscess formation occurs in the setting of an acute inflammatory response to an infectious organism, resulting in an organized collection of pus, necrotic cellular debris, and infectious organisms present on histology. A bacterial abscess presents with cutaneous erythema, warmth, fluctuance, and purulent drainage, often following inoculation from an injury such as a spider bite, puncture, or abrasion. Systemic symptoms including fever, tachycardia, and leukocytosis are often but not necessarily present. Most commonly, abscess formation is acute and results from a bacterial infection of the skin. The two most common pathogens to cause bacterial infections of the skin are Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes (group A). S. aureus is most likely to cause a bacterial abscess. It also causes impetigo, erysipelas, and folliculitis. Other less common organisms include Clostridium perfringens, which infects an open wound and causes necrotizing fasciitis, Enterococcus faecalis, which causes nosocomial infections, and Pasteurella multocida, which causes infections secondary to cat and dog bites. Incision and drainage would be appropriate therapy for an abscess to

release pus and debris to control the source of the infection. While the patient may also require oral antibiotics, without incision and drainage the oral antibiotics will not effectively penetrate the abscess wall; thus, it is the most important next step.

wrongAnswers.A: Biopsy of the affected area (Choice A) is not necessary in this case. Skin biopsy is performed when there is diagnostic uncertainty about the cause of a skin finding and can be used to obtain a sample for culture. It involves surgically removing a small core of skin and submitting it for pathology in formalin or for tissue culture in sterile saline. In this case, the diagnosis of bacterial abscess is clinical, and a biopsy is unnecessary.
wrongAnswers.C: Oral antibiotic therapy (Choice C) is inadequate in this case without appropriate surgical drainage of the bacterial abscess. While the patient may receive oral antibiotic therapy following incision and drainage, the bacterial source control provided by the surgical procedure is more critical than antibiotic therapy alone.
wrongAnswers.D: Topical corticosteroid therapy (Choice D) is used to treat inflammatory processes of the skin including dermatitis, psoriasis, and lichen planus. While the presence of erythema around the abscess clearly indicates inflammation, treating this inflammation with topical corticosteroids without treating the underlying cause, a bacterial abscess, will be ineffective.
wrongAnswers.E: X-ray of the right knee (Choice E) is not necessary in this case because there is no suggestion of bony involvement of the infection. X-ray of the right knee will not provide any information about the soft tissue surrounding the abscess. Imaging is unnecessary in this case, but if x-ray evaluation of the soft tissue was necessary, an MRI would be more appropriate.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 9 hours after she was bitten on the right forearm by another woman during an altercation in a bar. Medical history is unremarkable and the patient takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows a 1-cm avulsion injury to the right forearm. The remainder of the physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient's wound?

The remainder of the physical examination discloses no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient's wound?
questions.subject: Emergency/Critical Care

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: The appropriate first step in management of a human bite is irrigation and antibiotic therapy. Human bites that penetrate the skin are at high risk for becoming infected with oral and skin flora, including Eikenella, Fusobacterium, Staphylococcus, and Streptococcus species. Viral pathogens such as herpes simplex virus and HIV can also be transmitted. Superficial infection presents as cellulitis with tenderness, warmth, and erythema, but deeper infection can occur, which may present with pain with passive movement, crepitus, and systemic illness. This patient does not yet demonstrate any signs of infection. In this case, wound management including irrigation, control of bleeding, and removal of any visible debris should be performed. The wounds should not be closed because this increases the risk for infection. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is appropriate, particularly in patients with wounds on the hands or face, if the patient is immunocompromised, or if the patient has a prosthetic valve, prosthetic joint, or vascular graft. The preferred empiric antibiotic is amoxicillin-clavulanate, which covers both oral and skin flora.

wrongAnswers.A: Antibiotic therapy only (Choice A) is not appropriate because wound management including irrigation is a key step in the management of bites.
wrongAnswers.B: Closure, whether in conjunction with antibiotic therapy (Choice B), alone (Choice C), or with irrigation and antibiotic therapy (Choice E) is not appropriate in this case because it increases the risk for infection. The wounds should instead be left to heal by secondary intention. The exception is for bites on the face, which is a more sensitive cosmetic area. In this case, only superficial sutures should be used because buried subcutaneous sutures are more likely to harbor infection. In general, however, closure of bite wounds should be avoided except in the most cosmetically sensitive cases (eg, young patient, face, neck, or sensitive location).

She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. On examination, the left lower extremity is held in external rotation and is 1 inch shorter than the right lower extremity. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.subject: Musculoskeletal/Orthopedics

explanationPanel.correct: C. Fracture of the femoral neck
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Osteoporosis is a condition characterized by the progressive loss of bone mineral density leading to decreased bone strength. This decreased bone mineral density often leads to fragility fractures, which can greatly decrease mobility and even lead to death in elderly individuals. It is usually asymptomatic but can result in functionally debilitating fractures with low-velocity injuries such as ground-level falls. This patient presents with inability to bear weight and left lower extremity held in external rotation, raising suspicion for a fracture at the hip joint. Femoral neck fractures commonly present with a shortened and externally rotated lower extremity.

wrongAnswers.A: Dislocation of the knee (Choice A) is a rare injury typically caused by falls from high height, motor vehicle collisions, or athletic injuries and can be complicated by neurovascular injury. Patients present with an obvious deformity to the knee with joint and ligamentous instability.
wrongAnswers.B: Fracture of the acetabulum (Choice B) or fracture of the pelvis (Choice D) can occur with blunt injury to the pelvis and may result in inability to bear weight, but they would not typically present with extremity shortening or external rotation.
wrongAnswers.D: Fracture of the acetabulum (Choice B) or fracture of the pelvis (Choice D) can occur with blunt injury to the pelvis and may result in inability to bear weight, but they would not typically present with extremity shortening or external rotation.
wrongAnswers.E: Fracture of the tibial plateau (Choice E) typically presents with a knee effusion and pain with range of motion of the knee. It would not cause extremity shortening or external rotation.

explanationPanel.correct: E. No further diagnostic testing is indicated
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Lumbosacral strain commonly occurs following strenuous exertion and is characterized by dull, aching lower back pain that does not radiate to the lower extremities and which is not accompanied by neurologic deficits. Most adults with acute lower back pain of less than 1 month’s duration do not require imaging, which is of limited diagnostic value and leads to unnecessary testing, medical expenses, and radiation exposure. Imaging may be useful for the diagnosis of persistent back pain, pain that is accompanied by severe or progressive neurologic deficits, or pain that is suspected to be secondary to certain disease entities, such as vertebral metastasis, spinal stenosis, osteomyelitis, spinal epidural hematoma or abscess, or vertebral fracture. Any patient with red flags of back pain such as neurologic symptoms to suggest cauda equina or conus medullaris syndrome, history of malignancy, traumatic injury, midline tenderness, accompanying fever or infectious symptoms, or history of immunocompromise may benefit from acute imaging. However, most patients with acute lumbosacral strain can be managed conservatively with heat or ice, massage, and light exercise provided the history and examination are reassuring and lacking red flags.

wrongAnswers.A: Measurement of postvoid residual volume (Choice A) may be helpful for the detection of urinary retention in the setting of spinal cord injury, cauda equina syndrome, or conus medullaris syndrome. This patient has no urinary retention, neurologic deficit, or other red flag finding.
wrongAnswers.B: MRI of the lumbar spine (Choice B) may be useful for the detection of myelopathy secondary to epidural metastasis, abscess, or radiculopathy. MRI is of limited diagnostic value for nonspecific lower back pain or lumbosacral strain and is not necessary for this patient.
wrongAnswers.C: Urinalysis (Choice C) may be useful for the diagnosis of urinary tract infection, such as cystitis or pyelonephritis, or for the detection of nephrolithiasis. This patient’s history, suggestive of an acute onset in association with heavy lifting, tenderness to palpation, and absence of fever suggest that these diagnoses are unlikely.
wrongAnswers.D: X-ray of the lumbar spine (Choice D) may be useful for the diagnosis of vertebral compression fractures, which commonly occur in elderly patients with low bone mineral density, especially among postmenopausal women. This patient’s age, history, and tenderness of the paraspinal muscles are more suggestive of lumbosacral strain.

Examination of the right lower extremity shows discoloration and a dislocated knee. Sensation is absent from the knee to the toes. There are no palpable pulses distal to the femoral artery. No motor activity is present. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.subject: Musculoskeletal/Orthopedics

explanationPanel.correct: E. Reduction of the dislocated knee
explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Posterior knee dislocation may occur secondary to posteriorly directed force against the proximal tibia, such as in the setting of motor vehicle accidents. Posterior knee dislocation places traction on the popliteal artery and branches of the sciatic nerve. Such an injury can result in potential neurovascular insufficiency to the leg distal to the level of the injury, resulting in permanent loss of function if untreated. Arterial injuries sustained during a posterior knee dislocation can include dissection, rupture, thrombosis, and intramural hematoma; pseudoaneurysms can also occur. Imaging, including arteriography or CT or MR angiography, is useful to investigate the presence of underlying arterial injuries and to facilitate operative repair planning. Prompt reduction of the knee dislocation serves to limit the extent of injury by relieving neurovascular traction, thereby minimizing damage to and restoring nerve function and arterial flow. Pursuit of imaging studies should not delay the reduction of the dislocated knee.

wrongAnswers.A: Measurement of ankle brachial indices (Choice A) is useful for the diagnosis of peripheral arterial disease and of traumatic arterial injury, but it should not be performed prior to reduction of the knee in this scenario, where clear pulse and neurologic deficits exist.
wrongAnswers.B: Venous duplex ultrasonography (Choice B) is useful for the diagnosis of deep venous thrombosis or chronic venous insufficiency.
wrongAnswers.C: Nerve conduction studies (Choice C) are useful for the diagnosis of nerve injury or demyelinating diseases, such as multiple sclerosis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, or Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.
wrongAnswers.D: Venography (Choice D) employs a contrast agent to evaluate flow and anatomical abnormalities of venous structures. It is not useful for the evaluation of popliteal artery injury in the setting of posterior knee dislocation.
wrongAnswers.F: Arteriography (Choice F) may be useful for identifying popliteal artery injury. However, pursuing additional imaging prior to reduction of the dislocated knee will lead to delays in treatment and will prolong the period of neurovascular compression.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 17-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents because of a 2-day history of generalized weakness and fatigue. She reports feeling light-headed upon standing and says she almost fainted earlier today. She also reports being very thirsty recently. She takes no medications and has no known drug allergies. On arrival, she is sleepy but easily aroused. She is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 50 kg (110 lb); BMI is 17 kg/m². Her temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 102/54 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 99%. Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes. Lungs are clear to auscultation. The abdomen is soft and nontender. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Serum studies are most likely to show which of the following abnormalities?

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) presents with fatigue, polyuria, polydipsia, shortness of breath or tachypnea, and diffuse abdominal discomfort, most commonly in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus. It is caused by the accumulation of serum ketones such as β-hydroxybutyric acid, acetoacetic acid, and acetone in the setting of insulin deficiency. Dysregulated fatty acid degradation and ketone synthesis occurs as a result of the relative state of starvation created by absent insulin signaling. Vital signs may show tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypotension caused by severe dehydration. Laboratory analysis typically demonstrates increased serum glucose and ketones, metabolic acidosis, and a high anion gap caused by the accumulation of unmeasured anions in serum. Metabolic acidosis is accompanied by a decreased bicarbonate concentration in the serum because bicarbonate is consumed in the neutralization of increased acidic molecules (hydrogen molecules) in the blood. Treatment is through replacement of insulin, volume repletion, correction of electrolyte abnormalities, and treatment of any precipitating conditions.

wrongAnswers.B: Phosphate concentration may be decreased (Choice B), normal, or increased (Choice E) on presentation. Patients with DKA often have a total body deficit of phosphate as a result of osmotic diuresis in the setting of hyperglycemia. However, the serum concentration may remain normal or even high since the lack of insulin and metabolic acidosis cause phosphate to move out of the cells and into the serum.
wrongAnswers.C: Potassium concentration may be decreased (Choice C), normal, or increased (Choice F) on presentation. Patients with DKA often have a total body deficit of potassium as a result of osmotic diuresis in the setting of hyperglycemia. However, the serum concentration may remain normal or even high since the lack of insulin and metabolic acidosis cause potassium to move out of the cells and into the serum.

However, DKA causes an increase in the amount of acid in the blood, which is buffered by bicarbonate. Subsequent metabolic acidosis occurs with decreased bicarbonate.

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Heat stroke is characterized by an increased body temperature that occurs when the body is exposed to high environmental temperatures and high humidity, and it commonly occurs in young athletes or in elderly patients with impaired thermoregulatory capacity. Excessive heat exposure and increased core body temperature leads to cardiovascular and neurologic dysfunction with secondary tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypotension. Vasodilation of superficial blood vessels may lead to multi-organ system failure, including hepatic and renal ischemia, rhabdomyolysis, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Treatment includes cooling of the patient with fans or ice water, continuous core temperature monitoring, and support of airway, breathing, and circulation. Heat stroke generally requires neurologic symptoms to be diagnosed (collapse, in this case), whereas heat exhaustion presents similarly but with an intact neurologic examination.

wrongAnswers.A: Anabolic steroid toxicity (Choice A) includes hyperlipidemia, mood disorders, aggression, and cardiac hypertrophy. Anabolic steroid toxicity does not typically lead to hyperthermia and acute cardiovascular instability.
wrongAnswers.C: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (Choice C) occurs secondary to certain classes of medications, such as antipsychotics, and is characterized by hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, and autonomic instability. This patient’s recent environmental exposure to heat is not consistent with neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
wrongAnswers.D: Rhabdomyolysis (Choice D) refers to the abnormal breakdown of skeletal muscle and may occur secondary to crush or compression injuries, excessive exertion, alcohol abuse, medication, or toxic substances. Laboratory findings include increased serum concentrations of myoglobin and creatine kinase. While rhabdomyolysis may lead to myoglobinuric renal failure, it does not typically cause hyperthermia and shock.
wrongAnswers.E: Sepsis (Choice E) is characterized by an inflammatory response to infection that in severe cases or septic shock presents with hypotension and decreased end-organ perfusion. Patients may demonstrate fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, and examination or laboratory evidence of end-organ dysfunction. This diagnosis is unlikely in an otherwise healthy patient whose symptoms coincided with extreme exertion under high ambient heat conditions.

explanationPanel.trap: Rhabdomyolysis and DIC can be complications, but neurologic dysfunction with hyperthermia defines heat stroke.

explanationPanel.whyCorrect:
The large, multi-lobular, subcutaneous mass at midline in the neck of this middle-aged woman with symptoms of hyperthyroidism is consistent with a toxic multinodular goiter. In this condition, thyroid follicles become hyperactive, either autonomously or secondary to antibody activation, and begin producing excess thyroxine (T4). This patient is acutely symptomatic from increased T4 with fever, diaphoresis, tachycardia, palpitations, and hypertension. T4 causes these effects by stimulating b receptors in the heart and increasing adrenergic tone along with the basal metabolic rate. She also demonstrates signs of chronic increased T4 such as a 15-lb weight loss over 3 months. Other symptoms, though not present in this case, can include proximal muscle weakness,

diarrhea, menstrual abnormalities, and insomnia. The treatment of symptomatic hyperthyroidism begins with oral propranolol, which inhibits β receptors and decreases the adrenergic symptoms of hyperthyroidism. Treatment also includes antithyroid medications such as propylthiouracil, iodine, and steroids, along with ablation or surgical intervention.

wrongAnswers.A: Calcium (Choice A) is not necessary because it will not address the patient’s excess thyroid hormone. Calcium does not play a role in the development or treatment of toxic multinodular goiter. The parathyroid glands are located on the posterior aspect of the thyroid, and a large tumor obliterating these glands may cause hypoparathyroidism and thus hypocalcemia. However, this is not seen with a goiter, and the patient does not need calcium at this time.
wrongAnswers.B: Iodine (Choice B) could worsen this patient’s symptoms if administered prior to blockade of the thyroid gland with propylthiouracil or methimazole because it would promote even more thyroid hormone production.
wrongAnswers.C: Prednisone (Choice C) may decrease inflammation in the thyroid if this patient’s toxic multinodular goiter is secondary to an autoimmune condition such as Graves disease. However, it would not address this patient’s current adrenergic symptoms, which need to be addressed before further therapy. Prednisone can prevent peripheral conversion of triiodothyronine (T ) to thyroxine, but this follows adrenergic blockade.
wrongAnswers.E: Thyroxine (Choice E), or T , should not be administered to this patient because it is causing her symptoms and would only worsen them.

explanationPanel.rule: Symptomatic thyrotoxicosis is treated first with propranolol to blunt beta-adrenergic effects.
explanationPanel.trap: Iodine before thionamide blockade can provide substrate for more thyroid hormone synthesis and worsen symptoms.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department by paramedics 30 minutes after his wife found him lying unresponsive on the bed. His fingerstick blood glucose concentration was 20 mg/dL (1.11 mmol/L), so she called 911. His medications are glimepiride and metformin. He has no known drug allergies. At the scene, paramedics could not obtain intravenous access and transported him to the hospital. On arrival, the patient is diaphoretic and moaning softly. He does not cooperate with the examination. His temperature is 34.8°C (94.6°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 8/min, and blood pressure is 134/86 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 96%. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. No skin rashes are noted. Now, fingerstick blood glucose concentration is 15 mg/dL (0.83 mmol/L). The nurses continue to have difficulty obtaining intravenous access. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management while awaiting intravenous access?

explanationPanel.whyCorrect: Intramuscular administration of glucagon is the most appropriate step in management of this diabetic patient with severe hypoglycemia and no intravenous access. The treatment of severe hypoglycemia in a diabetic patient requires administration of either carbohydrates or glucagon. If intravenous access is available, carbohydrates can easily be given as 50% dextrose. However, in this case, intramuscular glucagon is a fast and safe way to reverse hypoglycemia in a patient with impaired consciousness and no intravenous access. After administration of glucagon, the patient must be closely monitored and intravenous access obtained because the effect of glucagon is transient. After intravenous access is available, a continuous infusion of glucose will likely be necessary. Any patient with hypoglycemia taking long-acting oral hypoglycemics ( sulfonylureas in this case) requires prolonged monitoring or admission because rebound hypoglycemia is common.

wrongAnswers.A: Application of a warming blanket (Choice A) should be included in the supportive care of this patient after his underlying problem has been addressed. Any delay of glucagon administration in this patient will increase his chances of death.
wrongAnswers.B: While the patient’s respiratory rate is low, bag-valve-mask ventilation (Choice B) is not necessary at this time given the adequate oxygen saturation of 96%. It is more important to address the underlying cause of this patient’s symptoms, which is severe hypoglycemia.
wrongAnswers.D: Oral ingestion of hard candies (Choice D) is an effective way of increasing blood sugar in a patient with intact mental status. However, this patient is delirious and cannot be given anything by mouth because of concerns about his ability to protect his airway if an aspiration or emetic event occurs. He may not be able to follow the command to swallow, and his cough and gag reflexes may be impaired, both of which increase the risk for aspirating the hard candy and irreversibly occluding his airway.
wrongAnswers.E: Rectal administration of dextrose (Choice E) is a less timely and reliable method of increasing blood sugar. This patient is experiencing severe neurologic manifestations of hypoglycemia, and the quickest method of increasing his blood sugar is necessary.
